name: Illness anxiety disorder (health anxiety)
dsmPointer: See DSM-5-TR: Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders — Illness Anxiety Disorder; ICD-11 places hypochondriasis with the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders.
summary: A persistent fear of having, or developing, a serious illness that normal test results and medical reassurance settle only briefly. Bodily symptoms are absent or mild; the distress comes from what the client believes they might mean. The fear drives safety habits that keep it going: body checking, searching symptoms online, seeking reassurance and repeat tests, or the opposite, avoiding doctors altogether. CBT for health anxiety, including internet-delivered CBT, has good evidence; coordinate with the primary care clinician so that care is consistent. For clinician review only; this is not a diagnosis.

durationGate.note: Ask how long the health fears have lasted and whether the feared illness has changed over time. See DSM-5-TR for duration guidance.

ruleOuts.label: An undiagnosed medical condition
ruleOuts.note: Keep the medical team involved and review new, changing or objective symptoms; health anxiety and medical illness can coexist.

ruleOuts.label: Stimulants and caffeine
ruleOuts.note: Can heighten body sensations that are then misread as illness. This app does not store substance-use information.

ruleOuts.label: Delusional disorder, somatic type
ruleOuts.note: A fixed belief held with full conviction despite clear evidence suggests a delusion; refer for psychiatric evaluation.

specifiers.label: Care-seeking or care-avoidant pattern (descriptive)
specifiers.note: Shapes the plan: reduce repeat checks and visits, or approach avoided care step by step. See DSM-5-TR for specifiers.

differentials.label: Somatic symptom disorder
differentials.distinguishing: Distressing bodily symptoms are prominent, not only the fear of illness.

differentials.label: Generalized anxiety disorder
differentials.distinguishing: Health is one of many worry topics rather than the main focus.

differentials.label: Obsessive-compulsive disorder
differentials.distinguishing: Intrusive fears of contamination or harm with rituals beyond health checking.

differentials.label: Panic disorder
differentials.distinguishing: Fear of dying during sudden attacks rather than a lasting fear of disease.

comorbidities.label: Generalized anxiety
comorbidities.note: Often co-occurs; screen with the GAD-7.

comorbidities.label: Panic
comorbidities.note: Panic attacks can feed fears of serious illness; assess them separately.

interventions.name: CBT for health anxiety
interventions.evidence: Tyrer et al. (2014) found CBT for health anxiety in medical clinics reduced anxiety; Axelsson and Hedman-Lagerlöf (2019) report large effects across trials.
interventions.note: Work on catastrophic interpretations of sensations, reduce checking and reassurance, and test predictions.

interventions.name: Exposure and response prevention for health fears
interventions.evidence: A core part of CBT for health anxiety.
interventions.note: Graded exposure to health cues (reading, hospital settings) with fewer checks and searches.

interventions.name: Coordinated care with primary care
interventions.evidence: Consistent, scheduled medical visits reduce unplanned visits and tests.
interventions.note: Agree a plan with the primary care clinician, with consent.

interventions.name: Mindfulness-based approaches (adjunct)
interventions.evidence: Growing evidence as an adjunct for health anxiety.

culturalNotes: How people describe distress through the body differs across cultures; some communities speak of heat, nerves, heaviness or a weak heart rather than of worry. Ask what the symptoms mean to the client and their family.

Past experiences of being dismissed or misdiagnosed by health services, which are more common for women, people of color and people with disabilities, can understandably drive checking and repeated visits. Acknowledge this before working on reassurance-seeking.
Do not assume that symptoms without a found cause are psychological. Keep the medical team involved and review new or changing symptoms.
Use a trained professional interpreter, not family members, and check that key terms translate with the meaning you intend.
If the client wants faith or spiritual practice included, follow their lead and get informed consent first (see the AACC Code of Ethics for faith-based counselors); never impose beliefs.
